title: THE FIRST PERSON JESUS CALLED BY NAME AFTER THE RESURRECTION WAS A WOMAN THE WORLD MIGHT HAVE OVERLOOKED
paragraphs: THE FIRST PERSON JESUS CALLED BY NAME AFTER THE RESURRECTION WAS A WOMAN THE WORLD MIGHT HAVE OVERLOOKED

Before the risen Christ appeared to the religious authorities, before Mary Magdalene understood the empty tomb, and before her tears had even dried, Jesus spoke one word that changed everything. And if you have ever felt forgotten, disqualified, ashamed, or too broken to matter to God, what happened in that garden may change the way you see your own story.
“Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.” — John 20:16 (KJV)
There is something almost unbearable about this moment.
The grave was empty.
Death had been defeated.
The greatest victory in human history had already taken place.
And yet, just outside the tomb, a woman was crying because she thought everything was lost.
She was standing only a few steps away from the greatest miracle the world had ever known, but grief had made it impossible for her to recognize what God had already done.
Read that again.
She was standing in the presence of answered hope, and she thought she was standing in the middle of another heartbreak.
Maybe that is why this story feels so painfully familiar.

Because some of us know what it means to pray until our voices grow tired, to keep showing up when our hearts are shattered, and to stand in the middle of circumstances that look nothing like the promises we thought we understood.
We know what it means to love Jesus and still cry.
To believe in God and still feel confused.
To have faith and still ask, “Lord, where are You?”
Mary Magdalene knew that feeling.
And on the morning everything changed, she was about to discover something extraordinary.
The risen Jesus was closer than she realized.
But to understand the weight of that moment, we need to remember who Mary was.
The Gospel of Luke tells us that Mary Magdalene was a woman from whom seven demons had gone out (Luke 8:2).
Seven demons.
Scripture does not describe every detail of what she endured, and we should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But the biblical testimony is clear: Mary had experienced profound spiritual bondage, and Jesus had delivered her.
Her life had been touched by darkness.
Then she encountered the One whom darkness could not overcome.
And everything changed.
There is an important truth here that centuries of speculation have sometimes obscured.
The Bible never identifies Mary Magdalene as a prostitute.

It does not say she was the unnamed sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet in Luke 7. Those identifications became popular in some Christian traditions, but they are not established by the Gospel accounts.
Mary's actual testimony is already powerful enough without inventing a scandal.
She was a woman whom Jesus had delivered, a faithful follower who helped support His ministry, a witness to His crucifixion, and a witness to His resurrection.
Her story is not powerful because we can attach the worst possible reputation to her name.
Her story is powerful because Jesus had changed her life, and she remained devoted to Him.
And perhaps that is where this becomes personal.
Because you do not need a sensational past to need a Savior.
You do not need to have committed a notorious sin to understand grace.
You only need to recognize that apart from Christ, none of us can rescue ourselves from sin and death.
Some people carry the consequences of public failures.
Others carry private guilt that nobody knows about.
Some are haunted by what they did.
Others are still bleeding from what was done to them.
Some have been delivered from things they cannot bear to describe.
Others are still praying for freedom from habits, bitterness, unbelief, or wounds that have followed them for years.
But the Gospel is not a competition over whose darkness was darkest.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and His mercy is greater than our ability to earn it.
Mary knew what it meant to receive mercy.
And she did not forget the One who had shown it to her.
When Jesus was crucified, Mary was among the women who witnessed His suffering (John 19:25).
Think about what that meant.
She had followed the One who gave her freedom.
She had seen His compassion.
She had heard His words.
She had watched Him restore lives that others considered hopeless.
And then she watched Him die.
The hands that had healed were pierced.
The voice that had called people into life fell silent.
The One she knew as Lord was laid in a tomb.
Imagine the confusion.
Imagine the silence after the burial.
Imagine trying to sleep when the last image in your mind is the suffering of someone you love.
Then came the first day of the week.
John 20:1 tells us that Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark.
That detail matters.
She did not come because she expected to see the risen Christ standing there.
The narrative makes clear that she initially believed His body had been taken away.
She came carrying grief.
And when she saw the stone removed, she ran to tell Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved.
The disciples came.
They saw the burial cloths.
And then John records a detail that almost stops the heart.
“Then the disciples went away again unto their own home. But Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping.” — John 20:10–11 (KJV)
But Mary stayed.
Do not rush past those words.
The disciples left.
Mary remained.
This does not mean the disciples loved Jesus less. John does not invite us to measure their devotion against hers.
But he wants us to see Mary standing there.
Weeping.
Waiting.
Unable to walk away from the place where she believed her Lord had been taken.
The Greek verb used for her weeping is κλαίουσα (klaiousa), from κλαίω (klaiō), a word commonly used for crying or mourning.
This was not a theological debate.
This was grief.
The kind that makes your chest ache.
The kind that leaves you staring at a place where someone used to be.
The kind that makes ordinary words feel useless.
And then she looked into the tomb.
Two angels were sitting where Jesus' body had lain.
They asked her, “Woman, why weepest thou?”
Her answer was painfully simple.
“Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.” — John 20:13 (KJV)
My Lord.
Not merely a teacher.
Not simply a miracle worker.
My Lord.
Even in her confusion, her words revealed the relationship that had transformed her life.
She did not yet understand the resurrection.
But she knew whom she loved.
And then she turned around.
Someone was standing there.
Jesus.
Alive.
The One she thought had been taken away was standing before her.
But she did not recognize Him.
John does not explicitly explain why.
Perhaps grief affected her perception. Perhaps the unexpected circumstances contributed to her confusion. Whatever the reason, the text simply tells us that she supposed Him to be the gardener.
And then Jesus asked:
“Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?” — John 20:15 (KJV)
Whom are you seeking?
What a question.
Not because Jesus lacked information.
But because John's Gospel places this extraordinary encounter before us with a question that reaches beyond the garden.
Whom are you seeking?
When your heart is empty.
When the people you trusted disappoint you.
When the future you planned collapses.
When you are tired of performing strength for everyone around you.
When you have money, attention, achievement, or approval but still feel something missing inside.
Whom are you seeking?
Mary thought He was the gardener.
She pleaded with Him to tell her where the body had been placed.
And then something happened that no sermon, no beautiful sentence, and no human imagination can fully capture.
Jesus spoke her name.
“Mary.”
One word.
No lengthy explanation.
No public ceremony.
No demand that she first understand everything.
He called her by name.
And she recognized Him.
In the Greek text of John 20:16, Jesus says:
Μαριάμ — Mariam.
A Greek-script form of her Semitic name.
She responds:
Ῥαββουνί — Rabbouni.
John explains its meaning as “Teacher,” rendered “Master” in the King James Version. It is a Semitic form of address expressing reverence for a teacher.
The exchange is astonishingly intimate in its simplicity.
“Mariam.”
“Rabbouni.”
Her name.
Her Teacher.
And suddenly the tomb was no longer the end of the story.
The One she had mourned was alive.
The One she had searched for had found her standing in tears.
The One she thought was gone had never been defeated by death.
And there is a beautiful connection to something Jesus had already taught.
In John 10:3, speaking of Himself as the Good Shepherd, Jesus says that the shepherd calls his own sheep by name.
In John 10:27, He declares:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
Mary's recognition in the garden echoes that truth.
The Shepherd knows His sheep.
And His voice is not powerless before grief.
But we must understand this carefully.
The passage is not promising that every believer will hear an audible voice from heaven.
It is showing us the risen Christ revealing Himself to Mary, and it reminds us that those who belong to Him are known by Him.
You may feel unseen by people.
You may have been forgotten by someone whose love you depended on.
You may be carrying a private battle that nobody around you understands.
But if you belong to Christ, you are not unknown to Him.
The One who knows every hidden sin also knows every hidden sorrow.
And the wonder of grace is that He does not save us because we have managed to make ourselves impressive.
He saves us because He is merciful.
Now notice something that makes this resurrection account even more remarkable.
In John's narrative, the first recorded personal appearance of the risen Jesus is to Mary Magdalene.
Not to Caiaphas.
Not to the Sanhedrin.
Not to the religious authorities who had opposed Him.
Not even to Peter or the beloved disciple in the scene John has just described.
To Mary.

We should not exaggerate the text. John is presenting his resurrection account, not providing a minute-by-minute list of every appearance Jesus made. The other Gospels preserve additional details, and Matthew 28:9–10 records Jesus meeting women returning from the tomb.
But John's emphasis is unmistakable.
Mary Magdalene is the first person John explicitly depicts meeting and recognizing the risen Jesus.
And this is not an insignificant detail.
In the ancient world, women often faced limitations in public standing and credibility, although the legal and social realities varied across communities and circumstances.
Yet the Gospel writers did not erase the women from the resurrection story.
They placed them in the testimony.
And John records that Jesus entrusted Mary with a message.
“Go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.” — John 20:17 (KJV)
Go.
Tell them.
The woman who arrived at the tomb in tears was now sent to announce what she had witnessed.
John 20:18 records her testimony:
“I have seen the Lord.”
Six words in the King James Version.
An entire world of hope inside them.
She had not merely found an empty grave.
She had encountered the living Christ.

This is why Christians have sometimes referred to Mary Magdalene as the “apostle to the apostles,” an honorary description of her role as a messenger to the disciples, not a claim that John identifies her as one of the Twelve.
She was entrusted with news that would change history.
And the center of that news was not Mary.
It was Jesus.
Always Jesus.
His death.
His resurrection.
His victory.
His grace.
His call to believe.
And here is where the story becomes uncomfortable for anyone who thinks God only works through people with impressive titles, spotless reputations, or religious influence.
The risen Christ did not need the approval of the religious establishment to make His resurrection true.
His victory did not depend on human recognition.
And His choice to reveal Himself to Mary shows us that faithful witness is not reserved for the socially powerful.
The Lord sees people whom others overlook.
He uses people whom others underestimate.
He calls ordinary believers to bear witness to an extraordinary Savior.
But there is another truth we must not miss.
Mary's tears were not proof that her faith was worthless. And her devotion did not make her the cause of the resurrection.
Jesus was alive before she recognized Him.
The victory was already accomplished before she understood it.
Her confusion did not cancel what Christ had done.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that truth more than anything else today.
Your inability to understand what God is doing does not mean Jesus has ceased to be Lord.
Your tears do not undo His resurrection.
Your questions do not make His promises meaningless.
Your exhaustion does not mean He has abandoned every work of grace in your life.
But neither does the resurrection promise that every earthly loss will be reversed immediately, every relationship restored, or every painful circumstance resolved the way you want.
The Christian hope is deeper than that.
It rests on the historical claim proclaimed by the apostles: Jesus Christ truly died for our sins, was buried, and was raised from the dead.
As Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.
And because He lives, sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is the hope Mary encountered.
Not a motivational slogan.
Not positive thinking.
Not a promise of a trouble-free life.
A living Savior.
And the same Jesus who appeared to Mary is the Christ whom the Gospel calls us to trust today.
Maybe your story contains a scandal.
Maybe your family knows what happened.
Maybe your name has been dragged through conversations you were never invited into.
Maybe you are ashamed of things you willingly chose.
Maybe you are wounded by things you never chose at all.
Hear this distinction clearly.
If you have sinned, Jesus calls you to repentance and offers forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
If you have been sinned against, your suffering does not make you guilty of another person's wrongdoing.
And if you are weary, confused, or grieving, Christ does not require you to pretend you are fine before you come to Him.
The Gospel speaks to all of these realities without confusing them.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our reputation.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He did not die to help us maintain a religious appearance.
He died to bear sin and bring forgiveness.
He did not rise simply to inspire us to try harder.
He rose in victory, establishing the living hope of everyone who trusts in Him.
That is why repentance matters.
Not because repentance purchases salvation.
But because genuine faith turns toward the Savior and away from the sin that destroys us.
And that is why grace matters.
Because none of us can earn the righteousness that Christ alone provides.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis), carrying the sense of favor or gift.
In this passage, salvation is God's gift, not a reward we can claim through our accomplishments.
You cannot buy it.
You cannot impress your way into it.
You cannot purchase forgiveness with donations, religious activity, or a spotless public image.
You receive salvation through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
So do not confuse grace with permission to remain comfortable in sin.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus also calls us to follow Him.
The same Gospel that announces pardon also calls us to surrender.
And if you are reading this while hiding something that is slowly hardening your heart, perhaps today is the day to stop running.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn to Christ.
Seek help and accountability where you need them.
Make things right where repentance requires it and where doing so is safe and appropriate.
Stop pretending that a polished appearance can heal a wounded soul.
You do not need another religious mask.
You need the Savior.
And He is not dead.
That is the part we must never forget.
Mary did not leave the garden saying, “I have learned to cope with disappointment.”
She did not say, “I have discovered the power of believing in myself.”
She said:
“I have seen the Lord.”
Christianity stands or falls on the risen Jesus Christ.
And because He lives, the invitation of the Gospel remains open.
Come to Him.
Not when you have fixed everything.
Not when your reputation has recovered.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come in repentance and faith.
Come believing that the crucified and risen Christ is sufficient to save.
Come because His mercy is real, His sacrifice is sufficient, and His resurrection changes everything.
And if you have already trusted Him, remember that your story does not end with receiving grace.
Grace sends us outward.
Mary was told to go and tell.
We, too, are called to bear witness to Jesus, though our circumstances and callings differ.
Some of us will speak to a neighbor.
Some will encourage a grieving friend.
Some will share Scripture with a family member who has stopped praying.
Some will quietly help someone who has lost hope.
Some will use a social media account that once carried arguments, distractions, and empty entertainment to share the good news of Christ.
And perhaps that is where this article becomes more than something you read.
Perhaps there is somebody on your Facebook friends list who feels exactly the way Mary felt outside the tomb.
They are still showing up.
Still trying.
Still crying when nobody sees.
Still wondering whether God has forgotten them.
They may never tell you what they are going through.
But a simple act of sharing the truth of Christ could open a conversation they have been too afraid to begin.
Not to make yourself appear more spiritual.
Not to collect approval.
But because the resurrection of Jesus is news worth sharing.
Send it privately to a friend who has been struggling with faith.
And if something in this story has reached a place you rarely talk about, I want to invite you to respond.
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers.
Sometimes the most sincere response is the simplest one.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ brought you from shame to forgiveness, from unbelief to faith, or from despair to renewed hope, share what you are comfortable sharing.
Someone reading the comments may need to hear that the Gospel is not merely something Christians discuss.
It is the truth through which God changes lives.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around a ministry.
Not to replace your local church, your pastor, or the fellowship of believers.
But to keep pointing people back to the Scriptures and to Jesus Christ.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who will never enter a church building unless someone first helps them see the beauty and truth of the Gospel.
There are believers who need encouragement to return to Scripture.
There are families searching for biblical resources.
There are people wrestling with repentance, forgiveness, suffering, discipleship, and the question of whether God can still transform their lives.
We want to keep reaching them.
For believers who are able to give, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.
Scripture encourages believers to support those who minister the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that giving should be willing rather than pressured.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
You do not have to give money to prove your love for Jesus.
And your worth before God is not measured by your ability to support any ministry financially.
Pray for the people this ministry reaches.
Point someone toward Jesus.
The Gospel has never depended on the wealth of its messengers.
Its power belongs to God.
And as we return to Mary Magdalene standing in that garden, there is one final thing I want you to notice.
Her story did not end with her staring into an empty tomb.
It did not end with her begging someone to explain where Jesus had gone.
It did not end with her tears.
It ended, in John's account of that morning, with her going to the disciples and announcing the living Lord.
The woman who had arrived overwhelmed by loss was now carrying the news of resurrection.
The woman who had been delivered by Jesus was now bearing witness to His victory.
And the center of everything was still the same Person.
Jesus Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One who offers forgiveness and eternal life.
The One who is worthy of our worship, obedience, generosity, and witness.
Maybe you began reading this because the title surprised you.
Maybe you stayed because Mary's tears reminded you of your own.
Maybe something about that single word, “Mariam,” reached a place inside you that you have been keeping hidden.
But please do not leave with only an emotional moment.
Leave with the truth.
Jesus is alive.
And the risen Christ is worthy of your trust.
If you do not know Him, turn to Him today.
If you have wandered, return to Him.
If you are grieving, bring your sorrow to Him.
If you have sinned, repent and receive the forgiveness He offers.
If you have been restored, tell someone what He has done.
And if you are still in the middle of a painful chapter, do not mistake the chapter for the entire story.
The resurrection does not mean every earthly sorrow disappears today.
It means death itself has been conquered by the Savior, and those who belong to Him have a hope that reaches beyond the grave.
Mary came looking for a body.
She left proclaiming a living Lord.
And one day, every believer in Christ will discover the fullness of what His resurrection has secured.
Until then, we hold fast to the Gospel.
We walk by faith.
We love one another.
We proclaim Jesus.
And we remember that the darkest moment in a person's story is never more powerful than the risen Savior.
Mary thought she had lost Jesus forever, but the One she was mourning was already standing beside her, calling her by name.
